To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of the Breast Cancer Risk Assessment Tool (BCRAT) to estimate individualized absolute risk of invasive breast cancer in African American women may lead to underestimation of the risk.

African American women are at higher risk of invasive breast cancer than white women and that the risk for African American women can be estimated using a model that includes breast cancer risk factors.

(1) the use of the 5-year risk of invasive breast cancer as a summary measure of absolute risk is not supported by the evidence; (2) the use of a 10-year risk of invasive cancer as a summary risk measure is supported by the evidence and (3) the use of absolute risk of invasive breast cancers in the next 2 years is not supported by evidence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods for the analysis of data from clinical trials, and with the design of clinical trials.
the development of a new class of non-steroidal anti-estrogens (NBAEs) that are more selective for ER than for PR.
the development of a new generation of materials that will enable us to build a new class of high performance, low cost, high volume manufacturing technologies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of a combination of the above-mentioned methods can be used to identify and characterize a specific set of biomarkers for the diagnosis of breast cancer.
the evidence for the use of tamoxifen in women with a history of breast cancer is limited and inconclusive.
there is no evidence to suggest that the use of the pill causes breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a model for predicting the individualized risk of invasive breast cancer in African American women that incorporates genetic, clinical, and lifestyle factors.

the results of the studies are consistent with our hypothesis that the risk of invasive breast cancer is higher in African American women than in white women, but the magnitude of the excess risk is lower than that observed in the SEER data.

we have demonstrated that the risk of developing breast cancer in African American women is higher than previously thought and that the risks of developing invasive breast cancer are similar in African American and White women.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of breast cancer is higher for women with a family history of the disease, and that the risk increases the younger a woman is when she is diagnosed in the family.
we can project an individualized absolute risk of invasive breast cancer for African American women, which is an important first step in developing a risk assessment tool for this population.
we can use genetic information to predict breast cancer risk, which is an important first step towards understanding the genetic causes of breast cancer.
